claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by nanoscale chemical ordering associated with surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Segregated surface regions enriched in lower-melting-point elements melt at lower temperatures than the overall bulk alloy.
Inert-gas condensation or similar synthesis can yield HEA nanoparticles with nominally homogeneous bulk compositions.
Such synthesis can permit slight surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Mild ion-beam sputtering can remove a surface-enriched layer and thereby suppress surface segregation.
Controlled oxidation or another passivation treatment can fix or reduce the segregated surface composition.
Surface enrichment in low-melting-point elements creates local initiation sites for premelting.
Surface compositional inhomogeneity lowers the local melting temperature relative to the nanoparticle bulk.
Changing the surface composition alters the local energy barrier for premelting.
Increasing the surface concentration of lower-melting-point elements will lower the premelting-onset temperature relative to as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Reducing surface segregation by passivation or sputtering will delay premelting relative to as-synthesized nanoparticles.
The proposed effect should hold for HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–20 nm in size.
The proposed effect should hold across HEA compositions containing elements with significantly different melting points.
The hypothesis is expected to remain valid in high-vacuum and inert atmospheres.
The hypothesis may fail for nanoparticles with strong chemical ordering or extensive phase separation produced by alternative synthesis routes.
Particle-size distribution, kinetic barriers to atomic rearrangement, and bulk lattice distortion may affect the quantitative shift in premelting onset.
Failure of segregation-reduced nanoparticles to show a statistically significant premelting delay, or observation of a shift in the opposite direction, would falsify the hypothesis.
